Author affiliations
a Department of Mathematics, University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa
b Department of Statistics, University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa

Received 11th May 2021 , Accepted 16th May 2021

Published 17th May 2021

This article is part of the themed collection: COVID-19 research 2020–2021

Abstract

The COVID-19 pandemic has affected the world in many ways. Mathematical models are useful tools to understand the dynamics of the spread of the disease and to predict the future trend of the pandemic. In this paper, we propose a simple mathematical model to understand the dynamics of the spread of COVID-19. We perform a stability analysis of the disease-free equilibrium and determine the basic reproduction number. We perform numerical simulations to understand the impact of various parameters on the spread of the disease. We also use our model to predict the future trend of the pandemic in South Africa.

Polygenic scores (PGS) are increasingly used in biomedical research and clinical practice. However, most PGS have been developed using data from European populations, raising concerns about their generalizability to other populations. This study aimed to investigate the generalizability of PGS in African populations, considering both genetic and environmental factors. We used data from the Africa Health Research Institute's (AHRI) population-based cohort study, which includes individuals of African ancestry from South Africa. We calculated PGS for 10 traits using data from the UK Biobank and compared them to the same traits in the AHRI cohort. We also performed Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses to assess the causal relationship between environmental exposures and health outcomes. Our results showed that the predictive performance of PGS varied substantially across different traits and that the generalizability of PGS was generally lower in African populations than in European populations. MR analyses suggested that the relationship between some environmental exposures and health outcomes may differ between African and European populations. Our findings highlight the importance of developing PGS specifically for African populations and considering both genetic and environmental factors when interpreting PGS in diverse populations. Cervical cancer is a disease that can be prevented and cured. But it is not the same everywhere.

In Namibia, cervical cancer is the second most common cancer in women. It is the biggest cancer killer of women between the ages of 15 and 44.

And it is not just a problem in poor countries. In the United States, cervical cancer is the most common cancer in American Indian and Alaskan Native women.

Cervical cancer is caused by a virus. The virus is passed from one person to another through sex. Most women who get the virus don’t get cervical cancer. But it can take many years for the virus to cause cancer.

There are tests that can show a woman’s risk for cervical cancer. These tests can find the virus that causes cervical cancer. They can also find very early changes in the cervix that could become cancer.

The good news is that there are ways to prevent cervical cancer. And there are ways to cure it if it is found early.

But many women don’t know about these ways. And even when they do, they may not be able to use them.

The human papillomavirus (HPV) is a group of more than 100 viruses that can cause different diseases in different areas of the body. Some types of HPV can cause cervical cancer, anal cancer, penile cancer, vaginal cancer, vulvar cancer, and oropharyngeal cancer. Most HPV infections do not cause symptoms and go away on their own. However, some types of HPV can cause genital warts and cervical cancer. Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide. In 2020, it was estimated that 604,000 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer and 342,000 women died from it. HPV is the main cause of cervical cancer. The good news is that there is a vaccine to prevent HPV infection and cervical cancer. The vaccine is safe and effective. It is recommended for girls and boys aged 11 to 12, but can be given to younger and older individuals. The vaccine is given in two or three doses, depending on the age at which the first dose is given. The vaccine protects against the types of HPV that cause most cervical cancers and other genital cancers. The vaccine does not treat existing HPV infections or cervical cancer. It is important to continue with regular gynecological check-ups even after vaccination. The vaccine is part of the National Immunization Program in many countries. This means that in some countries the vaccine is free or subsidized. It is important to talk to a doctor or health professional to know more about the vaccine and the HPV infection. Source: American Cancer Society

samples.ref: ተመራማሪዎች የሄፐታይተስ ቢ ህክምናን ለማሻሻል መመሪያ ይሰጣሉ፡፡
samples.hyp:
Researchers give guidelines to improve hepatitis B treatment
1 min to read
Jan 12, 2022
The first international guidelines for the treatment of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in children and adolescents have been published in The Journal of Hepatology, the official journal of the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL), and are accompanied by a position statement from EASL.
The guidelines were developed by a multidisciplinary team of experts from 12 countries, led by Professor Annalisa Craxì from Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, Italy, and Professor M. Zanetti from the University of Verona, Italy.
Hepatitis B is a serious disease that can lead to chronic infection, cirrhosis and liver cancer. Each year, it causes 887,000 deaths worldwide. In 2019, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that 1.5 million children were infected with HBV. Hepatitis B is 100 times more common in Africa and Asia than in Europe and America.
Professor Craxì commented: “The treatment of children and adolescents with hepatitis B virus infection is complex and requires a multidisciplinary approach. The aim of our guidelines is to provide a practical framework for clinicians to manage these patients. We hope that they will improve the consistency and quality of care for children and adolescents with hepatitis B worldwide.”

• Screening of family members of children with HBV infection
• Antiviral treatment of children and adolescents with chronic HBV infection

Abstract: The study assessed the impact of insecurity on women's entrepreneurial activities in Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State. The study adopted a descriptive survey design. The population of the study comprised 1,000 women entrepreneurs in Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State. The sample size of the study was 100 women entrepreneurs. Stratified random sampling technique was used to select the sample for the study. Data were collected with the aid of a structured questionnaire which was administered on the respondents. The instrument used for data collection was valid and reliable. The Cronbach alpha reliability coefficient of 0.85 was established. Data collected were analysed using simple percentages and frequencies. The major findings of the study are that insecurity has affected women's entrepreneurial activities in Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State. The study recommended that government should provide security to women entrepreneurs in the area.

BACKGROUND: Adequate concentrations of selenium (Se), copper (Cu) and zinc (Zn) are essential for the maintenance of a healthy pregnancy. AIM: To determine the association between maternal serum concentrations of Se, Cu and Zn and the risk of spontaneous preterm birth (sPTB). METHODS: This was a case-control study conducted at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital, Blantyre, Malawi. Singleton pregnant women aged 15-49 years attending antenatal clinic for the first time were eligible. Cases (n = 200) were women who delivered at <37 weeks of gestation and controls (n = 200) were women who delivered at ≥37 weeks of gestation. Serum Se, Cu and Zn concentrations were measured

Homing Behavior, Site Fidelity and Territoriality of the Pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya
English:
Homing Behavior, Site Fidelity and Territoriality of the Pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya

The pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) is a small, flat tortoise endemic to Kenya and Tanzania. It is well adapted to life in rocky habitats and is known for its ability to squeeze into small crevices for shelter. Despite its popularity in the pet trade, there is limited information on its natural behavior in the wild.

This study aimed to investigate the homing behavior, site fidelity, and territoriality of the pancake tortoise in its natural habitat in Kenya. We tracked 12 tortoises using GPS telemetry over a period of six months. We recorded their movements, home ranges, and interactions with other tortoises.

Our results showed that the pancake tortoise has a strong homing behavior, returning to its home range after being displaced by up to 1 km. The tortoises also exhibited site fidelity, returning to the same locations repeatedly within their home range. However, we found no evidence of territorial behavior, as tortoises did not show aggression towards each other or defend specific areas.

These findings provide new insights into the natural behavior of the pancake tortoise and highlight the importance of preserving its rocky habitat. Further research is needed to understand the factors that influence its movement patterns and social behavior.

The researchers fitted 20 radiotransmitters to 10 pairs of radiomarked male and female Egyptian tortoises (Testudo kleinzi) and tracked their movements over a period of 10 months. The study was carried out in the desert areas of southern Israel, where the tortoises live in burrows during the winter and emerge in the spring to feed on wild plants.
The researchers found that the tortoises were able to return to their home burrows from distances of up to 10 km. The return journeys were made in a straight line, suggesting the tortoises were using a ‘cognitive map’ to find their way back to their burrows. The researchers also found that the tortoises were able to find their way back to a second burrow they had used in the past, even though this burrow was 100 m away from their home burrow.
The researchers say their findings suggest that Egyptian tortoises have a remarkable ability to navigate over moderate distances. They say this ability is likely to be important for tortoises that wander away from their home range in search of food or mates. The researchers also suggest that the ability to make ‘cognitive maps’ may be more widespread in tortoises than previously thought.
The study is published in the journal Animal Behaviour.

The primary endpoint was 24-week CD4+ T-cell count. The geometric mean CD4+ T-cell count was 480 cells/μL in the 1.5 mg/kg group, 459 cells/μL in the 30 mg/kg group, and 316 cells/μL in the 10 mg/kg group (P = 0.04 compared with the 1.5 mg/kg group). The 30 mg/kg rifampicin regimen was well tolerated.

A shorter, higher-dose regimen of rifampicin was non-inferior to the standard regimen of rifampicin for the treatment of HIV-positive adults with tuberculous meningitis. A shorter, lower-dose regimen of rifampicin was inferior.

English:
Tuberculosis meningitis is a severe form of tuberculosis that affects the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord. It is a life-threatening condition that requires immediate medical attention. People with HIV are at a higher risk of developing tuberculosis meningitis, and it is often difficult to treat. The standard treatment for tuberculosis meningitis involves a combination of several drugs, including rifampicin, which is a first-line treatment for tuberculosis. However, the standard dose of rifampicin may not be sufficient to treat tuberculosis meningitis in HIV patients. In a recent study, researchers investigated whether high doses of rifampicin could improve outcomes in HIV patients with tuberculosis meningitis. The study involved 150 patients with HIV and tuberculosis meningitis who were randomly assigned to receive either the standard dose of rifampicin or a high dose of rifampicin. The researchers found that patients who received the high dose of rifampicin had a significantly lower risk of death compared to those who received the standard dose. Additionally, patients who received the high dose of rifampicin were more likely to have a complete response to treatment, meaning that the tuberculosis meningitis was fully resolved. The study also found that the high dose of rifampicin was well-tolerated by patients, with no significant increase in side effects compared to the standard dose. These findings suggest that high doses of rifampicin may be a promising treatment option for HIV patients with tuberculosis meningitis. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings and to determine the optimal dose and duration of treatment. Overall, this study provides important evidence that supports the need for further research into the use of high doses of rifampicin in the treatment of tuberculosis meningitis in HIV patients. By improving outcomes for these patients, we can reduce the burden of this devastating disease and improve the quality of life for those affected.

Biochar and compost improve soil quality for crops

Soil degradation is a major problem in many parts of the world, and it is particularly acute in areas where agriculture is the main source of income. In these areas, the soil is often depleted of nutrients and organic matter, making it difficult for crops to grow. In some cases, the soil may even be so degraded that it is no longer suitable for agriculture.

There are a number of ways to improve soil quality, but one of the most effective is to add biochar and compost. Biochar is a type of charcoal that is made from plant material, and it has a number of benefits for soil. It can help to improve soil structure, increase water retention, and provide nutrients for plants. Compost is a mixture of organic matter that has been decomposed by microorganisms. It can also help to improve soil structure, increase water retention, and provide nutrients for plants.

When biochar and compost are added to soil, they can help to improve its quality in a number of ways. They can help to increase the amount of organic matter in the soil, which can improve its structure and water retention. They can also help to provide nutrients for plants, which can improve their growth and yield.

In addition to improving soil quality, biochar and compost can also help to reduce the amount of fertilizer that is needed for crops. This is because they can provide some of the nutrients that plants need, which can reduce the need for synthetic fertilizers.

There are a number of ways to add biochar and compost to soil. One way is to mix them into the soil before planting. Another way is to apply them as a top dressing after the plants have been established. It is important to follow the instructions on the product label when adding biochar and compost to soil.

Overall, biochar and compost are two effective ways to improve soil quality for crops. They can help to increase the amount of organic matter in the soil, improve its structure and water retention, and provide nutrients for plants. In addition, they can help to reduce the amount of fertilizer that is needed for crops. If you are looking for a way to improve the quality of your soil, biochar and compost are a good option to consider.

The GfK BAROMETER WEATHER app study, conducted across 18 countries in the first half of 2022, surveyed 18,000+ consumers on their use of weather forecasting apps. The study measured how easy a preferred weather forecasting service was to use, and how accurate and consistent its predictions were. How accurate were the forecasts from your preferred weather forecasting app?

On a scale of 0-10, the average score given to ‘how consistent the forecasts were from your preferred weather forecasting app’ was 6.0. The highest score was recorded in Mexico (6.7), while the lowest was in Argentina (5.5). 

How often do you consult the weather forecast? 

The average number of times per day that consumers consult the weather forecast was 4.4. The highest figure was recorded in Japan (5.5), while the lowest was in Argentina (3.5).

A Participatory Approach to Assessing the Climate-Smartness of Agricultural Interventions
Agricultural interventions are increasingly being expected to contribute to the multiple and interconnected challenges of food security, climate change adaptation, and mitigation. To support this, a new guidance document was developed by the Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) Alliance to help countries assess the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions. The document was based on a desk review of existing guidance and tools, as well as consultations with experts and practitioners. The document was then piloted in two countries. This paper presents the results of the desk review, the main features of the pilot, and lessons learned. The paper concludes that the participatory approach proposed in the guidance document is a useful tool for assessing the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions, but that it should be used in combination with other methods and tools, and that it should be further tested and refined.

The current treatment options for odontogenic keratocyst include enucleation, marsupialization, and marginal resection. Enucleation is the removal of the cyst and its lining, while marsupialization involves creating a communication between the cyst and the oral cavity to allow for drainage. Marginal resection involves removing the cyst and a margin of normal tissue around it. The choice of treatment depends on various factors such as the size and location of the cyst, the number of recurrences, and the patient’s age and overall health. Enucleation is generally considered the standard treatment, but marsupialization may be preferred in certain cases, such as when the cyst is located in a difficult-to-reach area or when the patient is at high risk for complications from surgery. Marginal resection is typically reserved for cases where enucleation or marsupialization has failed or is not feasible. However, there is ongoing debate regarding the most appropriate treatment for odontogenic keratocyst, with some researchers advocating for more aggressive surgical approaches and others emphasizing the importance of minimizing morbidity and preserving function. Ultimately, the choice of treatment should be individualized and based on a careful consideration of the patient’s specific circumstances and preferences.1

English: The study was conducted in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Makkah Armed Forces Hospital, Makkah, Saudi Arabia. The study was conducted from January 2019 to June 2019. This was a prospective observational study. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Armed Forces Hospital, Makkah, Saudi Arabia. Informed written consent was obtained from all the participants. The inclusion criteria were women of reproductive age with a history of at least one previous pregnancy and those who were currently pregnant. The exclusion criteria were women who had a history of more than three previous pregnancies, those who had a previous cesarean section, and those who had any other obstetric surgery. The data were collected using a pretested, semi-structured, self-administered questionnaire. The questionnaire was prepared by searching the literature and consulting experts in the field. The questionnaire was pretested on 30 women who were not included in the study. The data were collected by asking the participants to fill out the questionnaire. The data were entered into a preprogrammed computer-based questionnaire. Data were analyzed using the SPSS version 20.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). The data were presented as mean ± standard deviation or number and percentage. The paired t-test was used to compare the preintervention and postintervention scores. The level of significance was set at P < 0.05.

Review of Relevant Literature
The following are the relevant literature and studies that will serve as basis of the study.
The study conducted by the researchers of the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) on the effect of different levels of fish meal, fish oil, and menhaden fish protein concentrate (FPC) on the performance, body composition, and sensory characteristics of broilers fed rice bran as partial substitute for soybean meal revealed that the study showed that the performance of broilers was not affected (P>0.05) by different levels of fish meal, fish oil, and FPC in diets containing 25% rice bran. The FPC is a palatable ingredient that can be included in broiler diets as an additional source of n-3 fatty acids.
The study conducted by the researchers of the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) on the effect of graded levels of rice bran on performance, meat quality, and meat consumer acceptability of broilers revealed that replacing up to 25% of the soybean meal with rice bran in broiler diets did not adversely affect the efficiency of feed utilization, final body weight, and feed intake of the birds. Broilers can be reared efficiently on rice bran diets if certain management and feeding practices are observed.
The study conducted by the researchers of the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) entitled “Formulation of Broiler Grower Finisher Diets with Rice Bran Using Linear Programming” showed that there were feed formulation softwares readily available in the market that can be used by broiler raisers in formulating broiler diets with rice bran. The softwares are Linear Programming (LP) based and Quadratic Programming (QP) based. The study further showed that LP and QP softwares produced similar least-cost broiler diets with rice bran. Broiler raisers can avail of the services of nutritionist or consult the feed companies in formulating broiler feeds with rice bran or buy feeds already formulated with rice bran.
The study conducted by the researchers of the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) on the effect of graded levels of rice bran on performance, meat quality, and meat consumer acceptability of broilers revealed that training evaluators on meat color and texture analysis prior to sensory evaluation improved the reliability of sensory data. The study showed that broilers fed up to 25% rice bran in their diets had acceptable meat with no fish odor.

The disease is characterized by fever, lethargy, and loss of appetite.
There is no specific treatment for heartwater, but supportive care can help to improve the chances of survival.
Prevention is the best way to protect livestock from heartwater.
There are a number of things that farmers can do to reduce the risk of heartwater, including:
  • Treating livestock with acaricides to kill ticks
  • Removing brush and other vegetation where ticks can live
  • Vaccinating livestock against heartwater

English
Towards definitions of critical illness and critical care using concept analysis
English
Critical illness and critical care are terms used widely in the literature. However, the terms are not used consistently and are often used interchangeably. This creates confusion for researchers and clinicians. To clarify the terms, the authors used Walker and Avant’s method of concept analysis to analyze the 2 terms. The analysis revealed the following: (1) multiple definitions of the terms critical illness and critical care exist; (2) the definitions are not used consistently; (3) critical illness is a medical diagnosis, whereas critical care is a specialized health care delivery system; (4) patient severity of illness is only 1 of the many factors that determine the need for critical care. The analysis of the terms critical illness and critical care is a first step in clarifying the 2 terms. It is hoped that the clarification will lead to more consistent use of the terms in the literature and, ultimately, to improved research and clinical practice.

Scientists study how malaria hacks cells to try and expand treatment options
Scientists are studying how the malaria parasite infects and hides in red blood cells to try and expand treatment options.
Scientists are studying how the malaria parasite infects and hides in red blood cells to try and expand treatment options.
© Wellcome Sanger Institute
© Wellcome Sanger Institute

Malaria is one of the world’s most deadly diseases, killing around 400,000 people every year. The vast majority of these deaths are in young children in sub-Saharan Africa. The disease is caused by a parasite that is spread by mosquitoes. Once inside the human body, the parasite infects and hides in red blood cells, making it difficult for the immune system to fight off. It also makes it hard to develop an effective vaccine.

Scientists are trying to understand how the parasite infects and hides in the cells to try and find new ways to treat and potentially prevent the disease. In a new study, published in Nature, researchers from the Wellcome Sanger Institute and their collaborators used a new method to look at the genetic material of individual red blood cells. They found that the malaria parasite uses a number of different strategies to hide in the cells, and that these strategies vary between different people.

This insight could help researchers design more effective drugs and vaccines to treat and potentially prevent malaria.

“Decades of research have gone into understanding malaria, but there are still many unknowns. Our new method has given us a much more detailed view of how malaria infects and hides in red blood cells, and I’m excited to see where it leads.”

Dr Marcus Buggert, co-first author from the Wellcome Sanger Institute

The parasite that causes malaria is called Plasmodium. There are five species of Plasmodium that can infect people, but the most serious ones are Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax. P. falciparum is responsible for the most deaths, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa.

Biological Invasions as a Component of South Africa’s Global Change Research Effort
Authors
Abstract
Biological invasions are a serious threat to the world’s biodiversity. South Africa is a global biodiversity hotspot and is therefore particularly vulnerable to the impacts of biological invasions. The South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) is mandated to coordinate the national biodiversity research effort. In 2005, the national biodiversity research effort was realigned to respond to the national biodiversity strategy and action plan. This article describes the role of biological invasions in the national biodiversity research effort and the contribution of SANBI’s Invasive Species Unit to the research effort. The article also describes the research capacity building activities of the unit and the research projects that are currently being undertaken. The article concludes with a discussion of the challenges and opportunities facing the unit.

Invasive species in South Africa

Invasive species are non-native organisms that can cause harm to the environment, economy, and human health. South Africa is one of the countries that are facing the problem of invasive species, as it has a high number of introduced species that have become established and are causing damage to the native biodiversity and ecosystem services.

The problem of invasive species in South Africa is complex and multifaceted, as it involves different drivers of change, such as climate change, land-use change, and human activities. These drivers can interact in different ways and at different scales, leading to different impacts and outcomes for the invasive species and the native species.

To understand the problem of invasive species in South Africa, it is important to identify the key drivers of change and their interactions. This can help to develop effective strategies for managing and controlling the invasive species, as well as for preventing their introduction and spread.

One of the key drivers of change for invasive species in South Africa is climate change. Climate change can affect the distribution and abundance of invasive species, as well as their interactions with native species. For example, climate change can lead to changes in temperature, precipitation, and seasonality, which can favor the growth and reproduction of some invasive species, while reducing the suitability of their habitats for native species.

Another key driver of change for invasive species in South Africa is land-use change. Land-use change can affect the availability and quality of habitats for invasive species, as well as their interactions with native species. For example, land-use change can lead to the conversion of natural habitats to agricultural or urban areas, which can provide new opportunities for invasive species to establish and spread.

Human activities are also important drivers of change for invasive species in South Africa. A new study of the SARS-CoV-2 virus in Uganda has found that the Omicron variant is more likely to spread in the country than the BA.2 subvariant of the Delta variant, even though the latter is more severe. The study also found that the COVID-19 vaccines available in Uganda are effective at preventing severe disease and death, but may not be as effective at preventing mild or asymptomatic infections. The researchers recommend more genomic surveillance to help us understand how virus variants respond to vaccines available in Uganda and other countries.
The study, published in the journal PLOS Pathogens, analyzed 1,000 SARS-CoV-2 genomes collected in Uganda between October 2020 and February 2022. The researchers found that the Omicron variant was the most common variant in Uganda during the study period, accounting for 60% of the genomes analyzed. The BA.2 subvariant of the Delta variant was the second most common variant, accounting for 30% of the genomes analyzed. The other 10% of the genomes analyzed belonged to other variants, including the original SARS-CoV-2 strain and the Alpha variant.
The researchers also found that the Omicron variant was more likely to spread in Uganda than the BA.2 subvariant of the Delta variant. This is despite the fact that the BA.2 subvariant is more severe than the Omicron variant. The researchers suggest that the Omicron variant may be more transmissible than the BA.2 subvariant, or that it may be better able to evade the immune response generated by previous infections or vaccination.
The study also found that the COVID-19 vaccines available in Uganda are effective at preventing severe disease and death. The researchers found that individuals who were fully vaccinated were 80% less likely to develop severe COVID-19 than individuals who were unvaccinated. The vaccines were also effective at preventing hospitalization and death due to COVID-19. However, the vaccines were not as effective at preventing mild or asymptomatic infections. The researchers found that individuals who were fully vaccinated were only 40% less likely to develop a mild or asymptomatic infection than individuals who were unvaccinated.
The researchers recommend more genomic surveillance in Uganda and other countries to help us understand how virus variants respond to vaccines and other interventions.
